subject: Hyperscaler baseline comparison — next experiments & benchmarks
messages:
From: Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.com>
To: Amit Shah <amit.shah@acme-analytics.com>, Lydia Gomez <lydia.gomez@dataforge.io>
Cc: Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 20 May 2027 15:10:00 -0700
Subject: Hyperscaler baseline comparison — next experiments & benchmarks

Thanks again for the demo today — good to meet the Acme and DataForge teams. Quick recap + proposed next steps so we can turn this into a runnable test plan.

Call highlights (short):
- You run most production traffic on HyperscaleCloud Inference API v2 (single-GPU instances), and you reported 6ms/ token average on short prompts but see spikes on long-context jobs.
- Primary use case: multi-turn customer support summarization with ~350–800 tokens per request and occasional long-document reruns (2k+ tokens).
- Key decision criteria: 95/99 latency, steady tokens/sec on batch inference, and predictable tail behavior under sustained concurrency.

Our ask / proposed experiments:
1) Head-to-head A/B: Redwood hosted inference (our recommended model variant + quantization profile) vs HyperscaleCloud v2 using your representative workload (see attached "acme_latency_summary_v1.pdf"). We suggest:
   - 3 runs per config, 5 minutes each, stepping concurrency: 1, 4, 8, 16.
   - Measure p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and CPU pre/post overhead.
2) Long-context stress: 2k-token requests at concurrency 2/4 to measure KV-cache impact and p99 tail.
3) Throughput sweep: fixed batch sizes (1, 4, 8) to capture tokens/sec/GPU and cost per 1M tokens estimate.

Hypothesis we want to validate (short):
- Redwood's workload-aware batching + prefix cache will reduce tokens/sec cost by >=20% at p95 comparable to Hyperscale.
- Hyperscale shows lower median but worse p99 for long contexts under moderate concurrency.

What we need from you to run the A/B:
- Representative payloads (we have the sample set but want them in your exact request format).
- Baseline Hyperscale config (instance type, model id/version, any custom plugins).
- A preferred 2-hour window next week when your infra can run the Hyperscale side (we'll run Redwood in parallel).

I attached a draft test-plan (test-plan-proposals.xlsx) with exact measurement columns; feel free to edit.

Next steps: can you confirm: (a) test window availability, (b) your Hyperscale config + any rate limits, (c) whether we should run from your VPC or over your VPN?

Thanks — I (Mina) will coordinate logistics; Connor will own the test harness. Marcus will join exec sync if we see major deltas.

—
Mina Haddad
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
mina_haddad@redwood.com
redwood.com

Thanks Mina — useful summary. A few clarifications from our side before we lock windows: 

- Baseline Hyperscale config: inference-v2.large-gpu (1x A10 equivalent), model: hf/longchat-v2. We run with dynamic batching turned on and a 512-token client-side max by default for user-facing flows. For long-document reruns we ship as single requests up to 2,048 tokens (server accepts up to 4096).
- Observed numbers from our infra (approx): for 512-token requests under typical load: p50 ~ 70ms, p95 ~ 210ms, p99 ~ 480ms. For 2k token requests: p50 ~ 1.1s, p95 ~ 2.9s, p99 ~ 5.4s. GPU tokens/sec varies with batch size — we generally see ~1,800–2,300 tokens/sec/GPU for mixed prompts.

Constraints: we have a nightly batch job 01:30–03:00 PDT that spikes GPU utilization — avoid that window. Other than that we can open a 2-hour slot on Wed 26 May 14:00–16:00 PDT. We can either run tests from our VPC (preferred) or give you temporary access credentials to an isolated project.

One ask: can Redwood provide the exact model id + quantization profile you plan to run? We want apples-to-apples configs (quantization can change latency a lot). Also share the harness (script + metrics export) you’ll use so we can ingest the same CSVs.

On data: we will sanitize and send a smaller 1k record sample (same shapes) by EOD.

—Amit
Amit Shah
Head of Platform Engineering, Acme Analytics

Hi Amit / Mina — quick technical note on the harness and proposed measurement definitions so we avoid ambiguity.

Proposed A/B harness (high level):
- Runner: Python 3.11 script (we'll share) that drives both endpoints at identical concurrency and request ordering.
- Warmup: 60s at concurrency 1 per run.
- Measurement: 5 minutes of steady-state per step (concurrency = 1, 4, 8, 16). Record per-request timestamps at client (send/receive), server-reported processing if available, and GPU metrics via nvidia-smi exporter.
- Repeat: 3 repeats per step; compute median across repeats for p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.

A few details / hypotheses to capture in the test-plan spreadsheet columns:
- request_id, payload_size_tokens, batch_size, send_ts, recv_ts, server_proc_ms (if reported), cpu_idle_pct, gpu_mem_free_mb, gpu_util_pct, run_id.

Hypotheses (to be explicit):
H1: Redwood's prefix KV cache reduces p95 for multi-turn reruns by ~30% compared to Hyperscale under concurrency >=4.
H2: For 2k token single requests, Hyperscale median is similar but p99 will be 1.5–2x Redwood's due to different attention kernel fallbacks.
H3: Total tokens/sec/GPU will be within 15% across platforms when both use similar quantization; differences larger than that imply kernel/implementation gaps.

Connor included a short excerpt from the harness (feel free to adapt):

> # sample runner snippet
> import time, requests
> def run_step(endpoint, concurrency, duration_s=300):
>     # spawn concurrency workers, each sending requests sequentially for duration_s
>     pass  # full script to be shared in repo

We can share the full script in a private repo link once Acme confirms the test window and gives us the Hyperscale endpoint details. Also — co-locate metric collectors (Prometheus) if possible so we can align metrics names.

Connor O'Brien
